outcome: No proof, counterexample, or AI-assisted progress on the uniform Pillai statement was found since 26 January 2024. The in-window items are a bounded-base quantitative result (Styer, arXiv 2402.04428, 6 Feb 2024), variants with Lucas, Fibonacci, convergent-denominator or polynomial analogues, and a neighbouring sum-form paper; the only solved instance (k = 1, Mihăilescu) and the classical fixed-exponent finiteness (Siegel 1929) both predate the window.
problem_asks: Unpacked from the statement alone, before weighing any event. (P1) Coefficients: 'for any A, B, C', i.e. all integer triples. The statement does not say nonzero, and with A = B, C = 0 and m = n the diagonal x = y gives infinitely many solutions, so C ≠ 0 (and presumably A, B ≠ 0) must be intended; flagged, not resolved here. (P2) Exponent pairs (m, n) of integers, excluding 'not both 2'. (P3) The claim that Ax^m − By^n = C has finitely many solutions, the unknowns being the bases x and y. Two scopes of P2–P3 are live and this record does not choose between them. Reading (a): m and n are fixed per instance, so the claim is that for each admissible (A, B, C, m, n) there are finitely many integer pairs (x, y). Reading (b): m and n are also unknown, so the claim is that the set of all solutions (x, y, m, n) is finite; this is the usual Pillai form (Waldschmidt survey Conjecture 1.6, with all four of a, b, x, y unknown in the notation a^x − b^y = k). The (2,2) exclusion is needed under both readings, because Ax² − By² = C is a conic whose solution set can be infinite. Under reading (b), the instance A = B = C = 1 is Catalan's conjecture, which is settled.

events.what_happened: Classical finiteness for fixed bases, with the exponents as unknowns: after work by Pólya (1918), Pillai (1931) and Nagell (1958), an equation the survey calls (2.6) is known to have only finitely many solutions (u, v), via Thue's theorem (Waldschmidt survey, ar5iv HTML, §2.2.2, read through a summarising fetch and not verbatim). The exact form of (2.6) was not confirmed.
events.delivers: For fixed bases and a fixed right-hand side, finitely many exponent pairs (Pólya via Thue). This is a different orientation from the bullet: the unknowns are exponents, not bases, so it is a different question that shares the equation's shape.
events.remains: Everything in the bullet: here the bases are fixed and the exponents vary; neither the bases-unknown statement nor the fixed-exponent statement is addressed.

checked_by.qualification: Number theorist; author of the survey on Pillai's work
checked_by.what_they_did: Digested the Pólya/Pillai/Nagell attribution in §2.2.2 of the survey

events.direction: Toward finiteness, but for a different unknown (exponents), so it does not cut on the bullet's claim.

events.what_happened: Siegel's 1929 theorem on finitely many integral points on curves of positive genus, as the survey applies it: for each fixed exponent pair (m, n) with m, n ≥ 2, the equation Ax^m − By^n = C has finitely many integer solutions (Waldschmidt survey, §2.1, read through a summarising fetch; the survey's phrasing reads 'each fixed pair (m, n) both ≥ 2'). The result is ineffective and gives no bound. Pillai's own 1931 work relied on Siegel's sharpening of Thue's inequality (survey §1.1).
events.delivers: Under reading (a) only: for each fixed (m, n) with the (2,2) pair excluded, finitely many integer (x, y), provided the associated curve has genus at least 1, or genus 0 with at least three points at infinity. The genus and point-at-infinity conditions were not verified for every (A, B, C, m, n). The survey's 'each fixed pair both ≥ 2' cannot be literally right for (2,2), so the stated range is too broad as written. Nothing uniform in m and n is delivered.
events.remains: Under reading (a): effectivity, and any exceptional coefficient sets where the curve degenerates, which I did not check. Under reading (b): the whole problem, because exponents are not bounded.

checked_by.qualification: Number theorist; author of the survey on Pillai's work
checked_by.what_they_did: Stated the fixed-exponent consequence of Siegel's theorem in §2.1 of the survey

events.doubts: The survey's range 'both ≥ 2' contradicts the (2,2) case, where Pell-type equations can have infinitely many solutions, so the fixed-exponent claim needs the genus condition for each pair. The genus condition for x^m and y^n curves was not checked from a primary source. This is the reason reading (a) is a classical theorem and not the open conjecture.
events.direction: Toward finiteness for each fixed exponent pair; this is the reading under which the bullet is already classically settled.

events.what_happened: Tijdeman proved that there are only finitely many pairs of consecutive perfect powers, which is the k = 1 case of Pillai's equation with difference ±1 and exponents at least 2. Reported by the Waldschmidt survey (§2, introduction, read through a summarising fetch). The primary paper was not read.
events.delivers: Finitely many consecutive perfect-power pairs, i.e. the k = 1 instance of the difference-of-powers equation. This is the only value of k the survey lists as solved before Mihăilescu.
events.remains: Every k ≠ 1 and the uniform statement. The k = 1 instance is covered more fully by the 2002–2004 Mihăilescu result (see that event).

checked_by.qualification: Number theorist; author of the survey on Pillai's work
checked_by.what_they_did: Reported the k = 1 result in the survey's introduction

events.what_happened: Bennett, 'On some exponential equations of S. S. Pillai', Canadian Journal of Mathematics 53(5) (2001), pp. 897–922. From search snippets only, not opened: for fixed nonzero coefficient and bases a, b ≥ 2, the equation a^x − b^y = c has at most two solutions in positive exponents x, y, with explicit conditions for at most one, using lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms. The UBC PDF returned a binary stream and the Cambridge page redirected without being followed.
events.delivers: Fixed bases and fixed coefficient: at most two exponent pairs (per snippet). This counts exponents, not bases.
events.remains: Varying bases, and the uniform statement under either reading.

events.doubts: The abstract was not read; the statement comes from snippets. A reader should confirm the exact hypotheses before relying on the 'at most two' claim.
events.direction: Toward finiteness, for fixed bases, counting exponents.

events.what_happened: Mihăilescu's proof of Catalan's conjecture: x^m − y^n = 1 in positive integers with m, n ≥ 2 has only 3^2 − 2^3. This is the A = B = C = 1 instance of the bullet. The first written argument is the manuscript circulated in April 2002 (MathWorld news item of 5 May 2002, search snippet), and a preprint 'Primary cyclotomic units and a proof of Catalan's conjecture' dated 2 September 2002 (cited in a Metsänkylä review in the Bulletin of the AMS, search snippet; the AMS page returned 403). Journal version: J. reine angew. Math. 572 (2004), 167–195, DOI 10.1515/crll.2004.048 (snippet). A simpler second proof followed (Bugeaud–Hanrot–Mihăilescu; Bilu, JTNB 2005; a 2006 proof per a review snippet).
events.revisions: Manuscript circulated April 2002 (MathWorld snippet); preprint 2 Sep 2002 (Metsänkylä snippet); Crelle 572 (2004); second proof JTNB 2005 (snippet). Sources disagree on the year (2002 vs 2004 vs 2003/2006 for various versions).
events.delivers: Restricted case k = 1 with A = B = C = 1: the only solution in positive integers with m, n ≥ 2 is (x, y, m, n) = (3, 2, 2, 3). Signs and zero values are not covered by this statement and are elementary (my inference, not checked).
events.remains: Every coefficient triple other than A = B = C = 1, and the uniform statement for general C. In Pillai's own form, every k ≠ 1.

checked_by.qualification: Specialist in Diophantine equations; co-author with Bugeaud and Mignotte of the 2014 Springer monograph on Mihăilescu's work (snippet)
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote Bourbaki exposé 909, 'Catalan's conjecture [after Mihăilescu]', Astérisque 294 (2004), pp. 1–26 (snippet, not opened); also an expository note on the second proof in JTNB 2005 (snippet)

checked_by.who: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Crelle), referees not named

events.direction: Toward finiteness: the k = 1 instance has finitely many solutions, and here exactly one in positive integers.
events.object: Not an exhibited object. The sole positive solution 3^2 − 2^3 = 1 is the Catalan pair, which the theorem shows is the only one.

events.what_happened: Heintze, 'Pillai's conjecture for polynomials' (arXiv 2201.10964, v1 26 January 2022). Proves that for any non-constant polynomial f there are only finitely many vectors (n, m, deg p, deg q) for the polynomial analogue of Pillai's equation. Published in Glasnik Matematički in 2023 (search snippet; the journal copy was not opened).
events.delivers: Finiteness for a polynomial analogue in which the bases are polynomials. This is a different question that shares the name.
events.direction: Toward finiteness, but for polynomials, so it does not cut on the integer claim.

events.what_happened: Cazorla García, 'On differences of perfect powers and prime powers' (arXiv 2312.09985, v1 15 December 2023). The abstract gives a method to determine the tuples (y, n, α) for which y^n − q^α has squarefree part equal to C1, for a prime q and squarefree C1, and says the case 1 ≤ C1 ≤ 20 and 2 ≤ q < 25 is completely resolved. The abstract page does not mention Pillai's conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Restricted cases with a fixed prime base q and a fixed squarefree part, for y^n − q^α. This is a variant, not the bullet.
events.remains: Every other base and coefficient, and the uniform statement.
events.time_since_posted: about 10 months at the frozen revision; about 33 months by 2026
events.doubts: A search summary said this paper states that nothing is proven unless an exponent or base is fixed. The opened abstract page contains no such sentence, so that summary is not supported by this source.
events.direction: No direction on the bullet: restricted variant with a prime base.

events.what_happened: Ibrahimov and Mahmudov, 'A Pillai-Catalan-type problem involving Fibonacci numbers' (arXiv 2401.08205, v1 16 January 2024). Addresses 3^x − F_n·2^y = 1 in positive integers, F_n a Fibonacci number. The abstract does not claim a general Pillai-type result. The listing shows a later version (v3), not compared.
events.revisions: v1 16 Jan 2024; v3 exists per the arXiv listing (not compared).
events.delivers: A Catalan-type finiteness question for a family in which one coefficient is a Fibonacci number, with the right-hand side fixed at 1. This is a variant.
events.remains: The bullet as stated, including the uniform statement and the general coefficients.
events.direction: No direction on the bullet: a variant with Fibonacci coefficients.

events.what_happened: Batte, Ddamulira, Kasozi and Luca, 'On a problem of Pillai involving S-units and Lucas numbers' (arXiv 2401.06555, v1 12 January 2024). Studies L_n − 2^x 3^y = c for n, x, y ≥ 0. The paper's published version in Periodica Mathematica Hungarica 91(1) (2025) is from a search snippet, not opened.
events.delivers: A classification of integers c for a Lucas-minus-S-unit equation. Lucas numbers replace powers, so this is a variant.
events.direction: No direction on the bullet: a variant with Lucas numbers.

events.what_happened: Styer, arXiv 2402.04428 (first submitted 6 February 2024). The abstract states that the Pillai equation a^x − b^y = r > 0 has at most one solution, with a known list of exceptions, when 2 ≤ a, b ≤ 3600. The arXiv title is written in sum form, a^x + b^y = c^z, so the title and abstract do not match. A Hrčak listing dated 31 May 2026 describes a journal version, possibly the same paper, with gcd(a, b) = 1 (search snippet, not opened).
events.revisions: v1 6 Feb 2024 (opened); journal version possibly 31 May 2026 (Hrčak, snippet, unopened). v2 not checked.
events.delivers: For bases a, b in the range 2 to 3600 and fixed r > 0, at most one exponent pair, with a listed set of exceptions. It counts exponent pairs at bases in a finite range, with the right-hand side fixed. This is a bound in a restricted case, not the uniform statement.
events.remains: Bases above 3600, varying right-hand side, and the uniform statement under either reading.
events.time_since_posted: about 2 years 6 months at the Hrčak listing's date; about 2 years 8 months to the cutoff of this record
events.doubts: Only the abstract was read. The journal version, if it is the same paper, would be a journal-level check that this record could not confirm. The arXiv title and abstract do not match.
events.direction: Toward finiteness for bounded bases, counting exponents; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Mittal, 'On a variant of Pillai's problem involving convergent denominators of quadratic irrationals' (arXiv 2508.11243, submitted 15 August 2025). Shows only finitely many integers c for which q_{α,n} − q_{β,m} = c has at least two solutions (n, m) with Q(α) ≠ Q(β), and solves specific instances completely. A search snippet reports a Glasnik Matematički acceptance on 9 July 2026, from the pre-copyedit PDF, which was not opened.
events.revisions: v1 15 Aug 2025 (opened abstract). Glasnik acceptance 9 Jul 2026 (snippet only).
events.delivers: Finiteness of c for a variant built from convergent denominators of quadratic irrationals, not powers. The abstract does not mention Pillai's conjecture.

events.doubts: A search summary said the paper states that Pillai's conjecture remains unproven for c ≥ 2. The opened abstract does not say this, so that claim is unsupported by the source read. Main theorem hypotheses were not read.
events.direction: No direction on the bullet: a variant with a different sequence family.

events.what_happened: Miyazaki, Scott and Styer, 'Handling some Diophantine equation via Euclidean algorithm and its application to purely exponential equations' (arXiv 2604.18991, first submitted 21 April 2026, v2 21 July 2026). The abstract treats the Scott–Styer conjecture on a^x + b^y = c^z and proves it for c = 7, 13 and 97 and, for primes of the form 2^r·3 + 1, except for finitely many cases. For the difference equation a^x − b^y = c it says only that the paper 'contribute[s] to the estimation of the number of positive integer solutions'. The abstract page does not mention Pillai's conjecture.
events.delivers: Specific cases of the Scott–Styer sum equation. For the difference equation, only an estimate of the solution count, with no specific result stated in the abstract.
events.remains: The difference equation a^x − b^y = c in general, and the bullet as stated.
events.doubts: A search summary said this paper poses Pillai's 1936 problem and calls it unsolved. The opened abstract page does not mention Pillai, so that attribution is not supported by this source; the body was not read.
events.direction: No direction on the bullet: neighbouring sum-form problem.

disputes.summary: The date of Pillai's conjecture is disputed. The survey gives 1931 for the earlier form m^x − n^y = a with the coefficient fixed ('This I conjectured some time back', §1.1), and 1936 and 1945 for the general a^x − b^y = k form (abstract and Conjecture 1.6, §1.2). Search summaries repeat both. The record uses the bullet's own wording and does not pick a date.

The abc route is conditional. The survey says the abc conjecture implies a quantitative refinement of Pillai's conjecture (§3.1), not the bare statement. Mochizuki's claimed abc proof is contested: Scholze and Stix (2018) reported a gap, and a July 2026 report from the LANA project, as covered by a secondary summary, says the step from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 cannot be formalised as written, while reserving final judgement. The primary LANA report was not readable. This is a dependency for any unconditional-to-conditional reading, not a priority dispute.

summary: I ran 41 web searches (verbatim in search.queries) and opened 12 sources. About nine more were unreadable from here: binary PDFs (the Bennett UBC PDF, the Shorey 2000 PDF, the LANA report), 403 or 503 responses (the AMS review, the Bugeaud–Luca NYJM 2006 paper, twice), a redirect not followed (the Cambridge page for Bennett), and a refusal (New Scientist). Nothing in the window resolves, or moves in any way that bears on, the uniform Pillai statement with bases and exponents both unknown. I found no source, opened or snippet-only, that claims a proof or counterexample of the integer conjecture for any k ≠ 1, and no source that links an AI system to it. The AI sweep (queries 4, 15, 16, 27, 35, 39 and 40, plus the opened Quanta piece of 3 August 2026 and the opened OEIS Open paper 2608.11941) found AI results on other problems only: the OpenAI unit-distance disproof, Erdős-site solutions, and an autonomous sum-product disproof. None of them names Pillai. The 'still open' status for 2024–2026 rests on absence of evidence and search summaries. The most recent opened source that states the integer conjecture's status is Waldschmidt's 2009 survey, which records k = 1 as the only solved value (§1.2, §2). Several search summaries attributed Pillai framing or status claims to papers whose opened pages do not contain them: Cazorla García (2312.09985), Haag et al. (2601.18138, on partition numbers), Miyazaki–Scott–Styer (2604.18991), and Mittal (2508.11243). Each is recorded as a discarded event with the correction stated. Within the window, the one event that concerns the bullet's own shape is Styer (2402.04428, 6 Feb 2024). It bounds the number of exponent pairs for a^x − b^y = r when the bases lie in 2 to 3600. It is a restricted case of the fixed-coefficient, varying-exponent form, not the uniform statement. The other in-window items are variants or neighbouring equations. Two of them (Batte et al., 12 Jan 2024, and Ibrahimov–Mahmudov, 16 Jan 2024) predate the frozen revision. Solved or classical items predate the window: Mihăilescu's theorem settles A = B = C = 1 (preprint circulated April 2002 or dated 2 September 2002, Crelle 2004; Bilu's Bourbaki exposé is a qualified digest). Tijdeman (1976) handles k = 1 for consecutive perfect powers. Bennett (2001) gives at most two exponent pairs for fixed bases, from snippets only. Pólya (1918) and Pillai (1931) handle fixed bases with exponents unknown. The decisive call is the quantifier scope of the bullet. Under reading (a), with m and n fixed per instance, the survey attributes finiteness to Siegel's 1929 theorem for each pair other than (2,2). I could not verify the genus or point-at-infinity conditions for every (A, B, C, m, n), and the survey's 'both ≥ 2' range cannot be literally right for (2,2). Under reading (a), then, the bullet is a classical consequence and nothing happened in the window. Under reading (b), with m and n also unknown, the bullet is Pillai's open conjecture and nothing happened in the window either. Either way, nothing that happened since 26 January 2024 moves the bullet. The abc route is conditional and disputed, as recorded in the disputes field. Two smaller points for the judging pass: the bullet does not state that A, B, C are nonzero, and with A = B, C = 0 and m = n the diagonal x = y gives infinitely many solutions; and no opened source dated after 2009 states the integer conjecture's status.
competing_reading: Read the bullet as the fixed-exponent statement (reading (a)). Then Siegel (1929) already gives finiteness for each pair, so the bullet is settled classically, the window contains nothing that bears on it, and the record's 'open' status would be wrong. Read it as Pillai's uniform statement (reading (b)), and it is open, with only the k = 1 instance settled. A third reading keeps C fixed but lets the exponents vary: this is the reading Pillai himself used, and under it the k = 1 case is settled and every k ≥ 2 is open. The record does not choose between these, and the judging pass should not treat the Styer bounded-base result as the uniform statement under any of them.
what_would_settle_it: The January 2024 Wikipedia wording and article history for this bullet, to fix which quantifiers the list intended. A primary statement of the genus and points-at-infinity conditions for Ax^m − By^n = C (Siegel 1929 or a modern source), to test the fixed-exponent reading's exceptions, including (2,2). The full verbatim text of Waldschmidt's survey §1.2, §2 and §3.1, since this record read it only through a summarising fetch. The Shorey 2000 paper (Publ. Math. Debrecen 56, 631–641, 'Some conjectures in the theory of exponential diophantine equations') for the exact form of its conjecture and the claim that it implies Pillai's conjecture. The Bugeaud–Luca NYJM 2006 paper, to check the scope of its results on Aa^x − Bb^y = c. A human arXiv search for 'Pillai' with 2024–2026 date filters, since the search tool returned no reliable listing. The Journal of Number Theory and Hrčak entries, to confirm whether the Styer journal version is the same paper. The primary LANA report, only if the abc route matters to the judging pass.
